label: HMRC policy paper · 29 October 2026
title: Business Asset Disposal Relief lifetime limit halves to £500,000 from 6 April 2027
summary: From 6 April 2027 the lifetime limit for Business Asset Disposal Relief falls from £1 million to £500,000. Here is who is affected, how past claims count and the rules for contracts signed before the change.
body:
On 29 October 2026, following Budget 2026, HMRC published a policy paper confirming a cut to the Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) lifetime limit. If you own a trading business or shares in your own company and you are thinking about selling or closing it in the next few years, this matters.

What BADR is now

BADR reduces the Capital Gains Tax rate on qualifying business disposals. At present, qualifying gains are taxed at 18%, and the relief is subject to a lifetime limit of £1 million of qualifying gains per individual.

What is changing

  • The lifetime limit falls from £1 million to £500,000.
  • The change has effect for qualifying disposals made on or after 6 April 2027.
  • The lifetime limit must take into account relief already claimed on qualifying gains in the past. So if you have used BADR before, those earlier gains count towards the new £500,000 limit.

Who is affected

HMRC says the measure affects individuals who dispose of all or part of their business or shares in their personal company, and trustees who dispose of business assets. According to the policy paper:

  • there are about 51,000 BADR claimants;
  • 75% of them are expected to be unaffected and will still receive relief on their entire gain; and
  • an estimated 13,000 individuals are expected to be affected.

Contracts signed before 6 April 2027

HMRC's paper refers to the Capital Gains Tax timing rule for contracts in section 28 of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992, and includes an anti-forestalling rule for contracts that are unconditional but not completed before 6 April 2027. Gains eligible for BADR will be subject to the £500,000 cap unless:

  • the parties can show they did not enter into the contract with a purpose of obtaining a tax advantage because of that timing rule; or
  • where the parties are connected, the contract was entered into for wholly commercial reasons.

Where either of these applies, a statement must also be made if the gain is more than £100,000.

Share reorganisations and exchanges

Some shareholders elect to disapply the normal share reorganisation rules so that they can claim BADR on an exchange or reorganisation of shares. HMRC says that where that election (under section 169Q of the Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992) is made on or after 6 April 2027, the disposal is treated as taking place when the election is made, and the £500,000 limit applies.

What I would do now

  • Work out how much of your BADR lifetime limit you have already used. Past claims reduce what is left under the new £500,000 limit.
  • If you are planning to sell a business, sell shares or close a company with significant value, look at the timing now rather than in March 2027.
  • Do not rush a contract through just to beat the date. The anti-forestalling rules are aimed at exactly that, and contracts that are not completed before 6 April 2027 may still be caught.
  • Keep clear records of the commercial reasons for any sale, especially where buyer and seller are connected.

The rules are still to be legislated in the Finance Bill, so details may change. If you are thinking about selling or closing your business, get in touch and we can look at what the change means for you.
